findings.finding: Recorded as fail deliberately, because the honest finding of this run is about my own tests. THREE assertions I wrote did not discriminate old from new behaviour and were caught by review, not by me: (1) plan.get("drop", []) read a key plan_gc does not return, so it could never fail; (2) the 'totality' test used a JSON array, which returns at the non-dict guard before ever reaching the encoder it claimed to exercise; (3) the numeric-boundary test passed verbatim against pre-fix code and generalised over a boundary that was leaky in the direction it did not sample. All three are fixed and each is now pinned by an empirical check — for (1) I reverted the fix and observed drop_ids == {'trg-human1'}. The pattern is the same one this run exists to correct in FIX B's fixtures, which is why it is recorded rather than smoothed over.

The mini-plan assumes the sweep-outbox caller only passes the id-set into `is_delivered` and never uses it directly. If the existing code ever iterates over `append_ids` or does a membership test outside that function (e.g., to decide whether to re-queue a line), replacing the id-set with a canonical-string set will produce a silent logic error.
findings.suggestion: Before implementing, grep `sweep_outbox.py` for any use of the returned set other than passing it to `is_delivered`; adapt the call site if needed, or confirm the assumption is correct.

findings.finding: The drift test (AC-5) intends to compare `triage.read_all_items` and `triage_gc._resolve_tracked_only` on the same damaged-status fixture. `read_all_items` normally consumes an entire triage file, not an in-memory list; constructing a shared fixture that faithfully exercises both functions without distorting their production paths may be non-trivial.
findings.suggestion: Write the test to invoke each resolver in the way it is called in production (e.g., pass a mini triage-file for `read_all_items` and the equivalent list of dicts for the resolver) and verify that the outcome is identical, not just that the same code path is taken.

findings.finding: The switch from raw-text membership to canonical-form membership for all parseable lines means existing tests that relied on the old matching for status lines or non-append events will fail. The plan explicitly calls for updating those tests, but hidden assumptions in integration suites (e.g., expectations about what lines survive the GC) could still break in unexpected ways.
findings.suggestion: Run the full `shared/tests/` suite (and any downstream test suites) early in the change to catch any assertion that implicitly depends on the old GC membership rule.

findings.finding: The mini-plan's `parse_delivered` returns `(canonical, text)`, where `text` holds only unparseable lines. That matches the new logic, but the function name and docstring originally said it returned `append_ids`. If the function is referenced by name in other tools (e.g., debugging scripts), the semantic shift may confuse future maintainers.
findings.suggestion: Add a brief comment in the function docstring explaining that the returned sets are now canonical-form and raw-text, and that the old id-only behaviour was a defect.  Overall assessment: The approach is sound; it fixes the three reported issues with minimal code changes, keeps the direction of risk safe, and deliberately avoids refactoring that would obscure the behavioural diff. The few points above are refinements that can be addressed during implementation without invalidating the plan.  SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: approve

findings.finding: The proposed canonicalization can treat materially different JSON text as the same record when either document contains duplicate object keys. Python's normal `json.loads` silently retains only the final duplicate key, so, for example, `{"event":"append","id":"A","ts":"T1","ts":"T2"}` and `{"event":"append","id":"A","ts":"T2"}` produce the same parsed object and canonical form. That conflicts with AC-1's requirement that same-id, content-different appends must not be dropped, particularly given the explicitly acknowledged foreign producer.
findings.suggestion: Treat JSON documents with duplicate keys as non-canonicalizable and use raw-text membership for them, just as for unparseable input. Implement a duplicate-key-detecting JSON decode helper (for example, via `object_pairs_hook`) used consistently for both origin and outbox membership paths, and add a regression test proving that duplicate-key variants do not cross-match.

findings.finding: "Semantically equal serialization" is broader than what the stated `_canonical` implementation guarantees. It handles object-key ordering, whitespace, and escaped-versus-literal Unicode after parsing, but Python preserves numeric representation types: `{"n":1}` canonicalizes differently from `{"n":1.0}`. A foreign producer that parses and re-emits a record through a runtime with different number formatting can therefore still leave status entries permanently buffered, contrary to the F27 intent.
findings.suggestion: Define the supported equivalence boundary explicitly in the implementation and tests. If FIX B/AC-2 only require whitespace, key order, and JSON escaping normalization, state that and test those cases. If numeric reformatting is intended to be semantically equal, use a deliberately specified numeric normalization strategy rather than relying on default Python `json` number behavior.

findings.finding: The planned new tests exercise `parse_delivered` / `is_delivered` directly, but the functional behavior at risk is the actual sweep decision under its lock. The change also alters the meaning of the first returned set while retaining tuple arity, which makes a parameter-order or call-site interpretation error easy to miss even if unit tests for the helpers pass.
findings.suggestion: Add at least one focused end-to-end `sweep_outbox`/GC test for each consequential direction: a same-id changed append remains in the outbox, and a canonically equivalent status line is removed. Keep the helper tests, but use the integration tests to establish the AC behavior through the real caller.

findings.finding: The plan assumes `sweep_outbox.py` is the only consumer of `parse_delivered` and `is_delivered` because the tuple arity is unchanged. Internal callers, test fixtures, or scripts can still depend on the former "append IDs plus raw text" semantics without a signature change revealing the break.
findings.suggestion: Perform and record a repository-wide reference search for both helpers before changing semantics. Update tests or callers based on the new contract, rather than relying solely on the unchanged two-value tuple shape.

findings.finding: Canonical serialization adds a full sorted re-encoding of every parseable origin and outbox object while the sweep operates in its canonical lock. Inputs include a known non-cooperating producer, so unusually large or deeply nested JSON records can increase lock hold time and delay other sweep activity. The assertion that `json.dumps` "cannot fail" is only safe while inputs remain ordinary JSON-derived values and within parser/recursion limits.
findings.suggestion: Reuse any existing JSONL record-size/depth limits if present. Otherwise, make canonicalization failure-safe: handle serialization/recursion failures by treating the line as raw-text-only membership, preserving the existing "retain rather than drop" behavior, and add a bounded malformed/deep-input regression test if the repository already tests such input handling.  Overall, the core approach is sound: canonical record membership correctly addresses the id-only append loss and raw-text serialization drift, and mirroring the status guard with a twin-behavior test is appropriately narrow. The duplicate-key handling and a real sweep-path regression test should be resolved before merging because this change is specifically intended to prevent incorrect GC deletion. SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: The canonical rule is strictly safer than the id-only rule it replaces ('direction of risk is safe'). — DISPROVED, round 1. Two same-id appends in the buffer: dedup_triage_lines keeps only the last at materialize, so the earlier never reaches a branch and never origin — and its canonical form is never in origin either, so it sits in the gitignored outbox forever. The old id-only rule drained it. Reproduced by probe.
findings.suggestion: Drain superseded lines, or accept and record the accumulation.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: Canonical membership compares like with like across the origin and outbox sides. — DISPROVED. Origin is decoded by run_git with errors='replace' (U+FFFD), the outbox by read_text_verbatim with errors='surrogateescape' (U+DCxx). A line carrying a non-UTF-8 byte therefore yields different strings on the two sides and can never match on either path. The old rule was immune for appends because it compared the ASCII id only. Separately FALSIFIED the adjacent hypothesis that a lone surrogate could raise UnicodeEncodeError out of json.dumps: dumps returns str and performs no encode, so the totality claim survives that attack.
findings.suggestion: Decode both sides with the same handler, plus a test seeding a tracked line with a raw 0xFF byte.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: allow_nan=False keeps fail-safety true for the WHOLE numeric boundary. — DISPROVED. It fires only on non-finite results. Underflow (1e-400 -> 0.0) and rounding (1.0 vs 1.0000000000000000001) produce finite doubles and still collide in the DROP direction. Also checked what does NOT collide, so the report is not a blanket: -0.0 vs 0.0 differ, NFC vs NFD differ, and escaped-vs-literal surrogate pairs denote the identical string so are benign.
findings.suggestion: Narrow the docstring, or reject floats entirely.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: The e2e tests demonstrate that the pre-fix rule caused data loss. — DISPROVED as written. The sweep COMMITS the refreshed line onto the iterate branch before the GC runs, so under the old rule the content was on a branch, not nowhere. Real loss needs the added premise that the branch is abandoned before merging, which neither test stated nor exercised — and neither e2e asserted anything about the branch at all.
findings.suggestion: State the precise loss condition and assert branch_triage_lines.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: The remaining new assertions are falsifiable. — Found the third of the run. test_numeric_reformatting_is_outside_the_equivalence_boundary passed VERBATIM against pre-fix code ({'n':1} has no event, so the old rule routed it to the text path and produced identical results) and could never fail against any variant of the new code either. findings.suggestion: Rename it to what it pins, or extend it to the leaky cases.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: The behaviour change is fully documented. — DISPROVED by grep. Three documents still described the DELETED id-only rule, in the run whose thesis is that a docstring claimed what the code never did: sweep_outbox's own module docstring, shared/glossary.md, and docs/hooks-and-pipeline.md — the latter two designated authoritative and mandatory-read by CLAUDE.md.
findings.suggestion: Update all three in this diff.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: The added lock hold time is defensible. — Could NOT break it, and corrected the brief in the fix's favour: the old parse_delivered already ran json.loads on every origin line, so the added work is one dumps per line. No pathological input constructible. Residual doubt is only that it was reasoned rather than measured, since this reviewer has no execution tool.
findings.suggestion: One timed probe over the real origin log recorded in the confidence calibration.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: The supersession hatch is worth its risk (round 2 of this review). — Argued plainly, as requested. BENEFIT measured zero (no superseded appends in the real log) against harm that is retention in a gitignored buffer git clean -x deletes anyway — and the identical shape of limitation (D2) was deferred as a card in this same run, so building a deletion path for one while deferring the other is not a consistent line. findings.finding: Claim under doubt: append_id's divergence from churn_merge._append_id is one-directional. — Holds on the strictness axis (verified across four orderings) but NOT on a second axis the docstring never mentions: the two parse different strings. superseded_appends called append_id(line.strip()) while dedup calls json.loads on the RAW line, and str.strip() is Unicode-aware where JSON whitespace is exactly ' \t\n\r'. Then tried to make it reachable and FAILED: classify_triage_text blocks such a line first, so the sweep returns invalid before the GC runs. Real but fenced — by a third module neither function mentions.
findings.suggestion: Key stage 2 on the raw line, or document the three-module dependency.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: The new totality test proves that input class is survivable. — The LEAF is total; the PATH is not, and the diff certified otherwise. churn_merge._append_id catches only (JSONDecodeError, ValueError), so a deeply nested line raises RecursionError out of dedup_triage_lines into sweep_outbox_to_branch, inside the lock, on step 5 — the abort three docstrings call unsurvivable. classify_triage_text has the same bare json.loads and cannot fence it. findings.suggestion: Add RecursionError to churn_merge._append_id and classify_triage_text, or narrow the test docstring and file the path-level gap.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: is_delivered's silent-reinterpretation hazard was handled by growing parse_delivered's arity. — Handled for one function and left open three functions below. is_delivered kept the same arity and types while parameter 2 changed meaning from an id set to a canonical-form set, so an old caller would pass ids positionally, get no error, and silently evaluate every line as not-delivered.
